title: Team Kickoff: A Vision for Our Future
leaves: The vision, the roles, what starts now, and the red flags written down.

slides.html:
DMV Digital Services

A vision for our future
slides.notes: Change the team name to whatever your team calls itself.

slides.html:
There will be more questions after today, not fewer... and that's ok.

The most important thing is that we lay some groundwork, and we know how we will work together to answer the questions that come up.
slides.notes: Name the growth zone up front. Growth sits in discomfort. If people slide into distress, we slow down. Ask the room to tell you where they are.

slides.html:
Where we started

A technology team focused on technology projects: predefined outputs, dates and requirements. New kiosks in the field offices, a new look for the website, a new vendor for the renewal form, all delivered on time. We were really, really good at it.
slides.notes: Honor the past before asking for change. Say what the team has done well, in their own terms. This is your story to tell; the DMV version is an example.

slides.html:
But then... an idea

A counter clerk, after sending another new-license applicant home without the right documents, asked: "What if we focused more on how people get through this, instead of what we ship?"
slides.notes: Credit a real person if there is one. A named colleague asking the question makes the change feel like ours, not imposed.

slides.html:
So we embarked on a new journey

How do we make this change to a more community-focused way of working?

  • One team and one roadmap for the DMV's online services
  • New roles: a product manager, a product owner, a UX designer and researcher
  • A steering group and an advisory group that meet monthly
  • Field office and call center partners who come to sprint reviews
slides.notes: List what has actually happened on your team so far. The DMV bullets are an example; replace them with your real milestones.

slides.html:
And now...

We have new team members, some with new focus areas, and a lot of new information coming at us. How do we fit all these pieces together?
slides.notes: This is the question the rest of the session answers.

slides.html:
Jot down your questions

5:00

We've all had questions about how we are all going to work together. What is the same, what is different. Take 5 minutes to jot down the questions you have. One sticky per question.
slides.notes: Silent writing, five minutes. Collect the stickies; they come back at the break.

slides.html:
As we go

Red flags: red stickies

Write down any concern that something might break or go very wrong in the direction I'm presenting.

Questions: yellow stickies

As I talk you'll have more questions. Write them down as we go.

Terminology: raise a hand

If a term or concept is unclear, stop me right away.

Space for grace

I've tried to balance different perspectives and needs, but I'm not perfect. Please give me a little grace.

We'll stop several times to address red flags. Yellow stickies wait until the break.
slides.notes: House rules. Point to the wall where stickies go.

slides.html:
This is a long-term vision

This is an ambitious vision for our future. We can't snap our fingers and make it true tomorrow. But we can start now and make steady progress, so we need to know where we're heading.
slides.notes: Lower the stakes: nobody has to be good at all of this next week.

slides.html:
Offering a digital service

We need to change how we see and do our work

From outputs to outcomes

From requirements to feedback

From incremental to iterative

From competing priorities to clear direction

From order takers to collaborative partners

From indirectly to directly serving the community
slides.notes: Six shifts, matching the system's story (doc 02). The earlier version had five; "requirements to feedback" is added. Each gets one slide.

slides.html:
Outputs to outcomes

The things we release.
The work we completed.

ex: launched online renewal

The results we achieve.
The change people experience.

ex: 75% of renewals done online in under 5 minutes
slides.notes: The examples are the DMV's. One from your own service would be stronger if you have one.

slides.html:
Incremental to iterative

We're used to big projects that take a long time and deliver value at the end. That still fits work with a clear end. For our services, we're shifting to smaller amounts of value, growing as we learn.
slides.notes: Wheels are a component. A skateboard is something you can ride.

slides.html:
Order takers to collaborative partners

The customer tells us what they want, and we execute.

We're given goals, and we work out how to reach them.
slides.notes: The sandwich shop is great at filling orders. The soccer team has a fixed goal and a path that changes every few seconds. Both are skilled; they're built for different work.

slides.html:
Requirements to feedback

Requirements

We write down everything up front and build to the list. We find out if it was right at the end.

Feedback

We put working things in people's hands early and learn what they actually need.

Some requirements are real: security, compliance, integration. Keep those. The rest are guesses worth testing.
slides.notes: New slide, from the system's six shifts. The faster-horses line works here: the skateboard teaches whether people need transportation at all, the scooter teaches speed, the bike teaches cargo.

slides.html:
Competing priorities to clear direction

Several people with #1 priorities, each trying to get their work done.

One clear lead, part of the team, directing us toward a vision.
slides.notes: Section leaders still contribute; there's one conductor. On this team that lead is the product manager, who owns the roadmap and the order of Strategic work.

slides.html:
Indirectly to directly serving the community

Serving the people who serve the people.

Serving the people in partnership with DMV staff.
slides.notes: We still serve staff, in service of the community. Residents use our websites and services directly, so we have to see the service from their side.

slides.html:
Is any of this different?

90%

the same

10%

different

Most of what we'll cover won't feel that different. Maybe 10% actually is.
slides.notes: Reassure: the skills people have still matter. What changes is where we start.

slides.html: But 10% makes a big difference when you change where you start: the core goals and the point of view.
slides.notes: Two ships leave the same port ten degrees apart and land on different islands.

slides.html: Pause for red flags
slides.notes: Read out the red stickies so far and talk each one through. Note anything you can't answer today.

slides.html:
One service

One team. One vision. One roadmap.

The roadmap

Vision and strategy

Goals and goal progress

Now, Next, Later

Quarterly commitments and sprint report

Discovery

Delivery

Enablement

Discovery: finding which problems are worth solving and which solutions will reach our goals.

Delivery: building the solutions, a slice at a time.

Enablement: making sure people succeed with what we release.

These are kinds of work, not separate teams with their own plans.
slides.notes: We see the service as one thing, from the resident's side. Discovery, delivery and enablement are the three kinds of work everyone does more or less of; nobody has their own roadmap.

slides.html: A soccer team is one team, but it breaks into forwards, midfielders, defenders and a goalie. Each focuses on their own responsibilities while passing the ball to each other. Our team works the same way.
slides.notes: Use the soccer team again: one goal, positions with focus, the ball moving between them.

slides.html: How the three kinds of work move together
slides.notes: Discovery runs ahead in small loops; what it learns feeds delivery's sprints; enablement teaches, listens and brings feedback back. All of it sits between strategy and impact.

slides.html:
How we will need to align

RoleWhoLeads
Product manager[name]Owns the roadmap: vision, strategy, goals, plans. Sets the order of Strategic work.
Product owner[name]Works with the delivery team on the backlog. Runs weekly request triage and the small request board.
Scrum master[name]Runs the sprint meetings and the capacity math at planning.
Technical architect[name]Feasibility, technical dependencies, and the order of Technical maintenance and bugs.
UX designer and researcher[name]Discovery research and design readiness.
Content strategist[name]Leads Enable: guides, training, champions, feedback from partners.
Development team[names]Builds, tests and releases; decides how and commits each sprint.
slides.notes: Fill in your team's names; one person can hold more than one role on a small team. Detail is in doc 14, Roles and decision rights.

slides.html:
Not all work is roadmap work

You have different types of work, and you look to different people for the priorities in each.

Strategic

Advances a roadmap goal, through discovery or delivery.

Ordered by the product manager

Technical maintenance

Keeps services running, healthy and secure, including bugs.

Ordered by the technical architect

Small requests

Bounded fixes to what exists, under one sprint.

Ordered by the product owner

Organization business (all-hands, mandatory training, timesheets) comes off the top before we count time.
slides.notes: An earlier version's buckets were roadmap work, functional duties (required, small requests, improvements) and additional stuff (training, department initiatives, other commitments). The system names them Strategic, Technical maintenance and Small requests, and takes organization business off the top.

slides.html:
How we split our time

Default 50/25/25, set each quarter at planning. It varies with your focus area. Examples only.

Mostly discovery

Strategic 70%

15%

15%

Default

Strategic 50%

Tech maint. 25%

Small req. 25%

Mostly running services

20%

Technical maintenance 50%

Small req. 30%

A guideline, not timesheet tracking. When the split changes, we say why.
slides.notes: The earlier version showed 70/10/10/10, 45/25/20/10 and 15/35/50/10 by team, and a 50/40/10 overall split. Updated to the system's three work types and the 50/25/25 default.

slides.html:
10 minute break

Review your yellow stickies. Add the ones you're keeping to the wall; we'll go through them during the break.
slides.notes: Group the stickies on the wall during the break so the next slide moves fast.

slides.html: Red flags and key yellow questions
slides.notes: Answer what you can. Park the rest with an owner and a date.

slides.html:
Changes moving forward

What can we start doing differently right away?

Quarterly planning

Line up the work we intend to finish each quarter, and commit to it together.

Capacity shares

Know how much time we actually have for each type of work.

A clear way to prioritize

Balance small requests, technical maintenance and roadmap work, each with its own owner.
slides.notes: Three changes, all small enough to start this quarter.

slides.html:
How do planning commitments work?

EACH QUARTER

The product manager prioritizes; the team commits to what it believes it can finish in the quarter.

Four half-day sessions: candidates, sizing, technical maintenance and capacity, commitment. Everyone commits out loud.

EACH SPRINT

Day 1: commit to a piece of the strategic work, some small requests and some technical maintenance.

Days 2 to 10: do the work, test it, deploy it. Everything should be deployable.
slides.notes: A commitment is a promise to try, not a guarantee. Some misses are expected; raising them early is part of the promise.

slides.html:
What happens with a request

Weekly triage: product owner, content strategist, technical architect, product manager. Answer within 5 business days.

OutcomeWhat it meansWhere it goes
Already on the roadmapIt's already plannedLink to the roadmap item
Small requestBounded change to something that exists, under one sprintSmall request board, ordered by the product owner
Large or strategicNew, bigger than a sprint, or could move a goalIdea log, for the product manager
Idea for improvementWould help people beyond the requesterIdea log, tagged separately
Will not doFails on feasibility, cost or strategyClosed, with the reason
Future considerationNot yes, not no; the requester is told we won't follow upStays in the idea log

Every requester hears back. Bugs skip triage and go to the technical architect.
slides.notes: The earlier version covered staff requests with four outcomes. Updated to the system's five, plus Future consideration and the bug path.

slides.html:
Next steps

1

Quarterly planning in December. Call it a rehearsal. We'll set our capacity shares as part of planning and make sure the plan fits them.

2

Then a weekly request review, so every request gets an answer.

3

Then sprint commitments and a sprint report every two weeks.
slides.notes: The first quarter will feel like a lot. It may not go well, and that's expected; doing it builds the habit. The DMV's was December; fill in yours.

slides.html: Pause for red flags
slides.notes: Second pause. Focus on what would break if we started next steps tomorrow.

slides.html:
Where do we go now?

Where do you need more clarity?

  • Specific roles and how they work together
  • The whole process with an example
  • A deeper look at something we covered
  • Examples of anything

You choose!
slides.notes: Let the room pick. The next two slides cover the most common picks: roles and the questions people ask.

slides.html:
Key role collaborations

Product manager and product owner

Work out tradeoffs as estimates and scope change. PM: which problems to solve. PO: how to break the work down.

Product manager and UX designer and researcher

Make sure we solve valuable problems with useful solutions. PM decides; designer leads the research.

UX researcher and content strategist

Talk with staff and partners together. Research finds root needs; the content strategist is the everyday touch point.

UX designer and developers

Settle design details and feasibility together, where changes might be needed.

Product owner and scrum master

Keep stories ready and sprints healthy. PO leads the content; scrum master leads the process.

Who to ask

What and why: product manager
How and when: technical architect or scrum master
Performance, career, time off: your functional manager
slides.notes: The earlier version had six pair slides. Condensed to the pairs in doc 14. The product owner and scrum master card reuses the developer illustration; swap it if you have a scrum master one.

slides.html:
Questions people ask

QuestionHonest answer
"We don't have the people."Probably true. This doesn't add work; it makes the work visible and limits it. Planning says out loud what doesn't fit.
"So now I have to work 90 hours a week?"No. You commit to what you can do without extra hours. If a plan only works with overtime, the plan is wrong.
"What's roadmap work and what isn't?"Only Strategic work is on the roadmap. Technical maintenance and small requests each get a protected share.
"Is there a separate roadmap for running things?"No. One team, one roadmap. Training and handoffs are Deliverables; running services is Technical maintenance.
"So projects are bad now?"No. A hardware refresh is a project and should run as one. Services that keep changing need a different way of working. It's about fit.
"Are we becoming teams within teams?"Discovery, delivery and enablement are kinds of work, not separate teams with their own plans.
slides.notes: These came from earlier teams going through the same change. Have the answers ready before anyone asks.

slides.html:
Pause for red flags

Then: start a team agreement, written as situations in the order they happen, and update it whenever someone hits a confusion point.
slides.notes: Close with the team agreement. Expect "where do I fit?" over the next few weeks; a five-minute show-and-tell per discipline helps.
